newsitem.title: USA: To IRA or not to IRA.
newsitem.headline: To IRA or not to IRA.

text.p: With Congress talking about a capital gains tax cut, some financial pros are talking about an end to the efficiency of after-tax Individual Retirement Accounts and annuities.
Both of these kinds of accounts allow you to invest after-tax dollars in vehicles that grow tax-deferred, until you retire or turn 59-1/2 and can use the money without paying penalties.

Critics of these accounts charge that they offer a lot of complexity for only a little payoff. When you take money out of an after-tax IRA, you still owe income taxes on the money that hasn't been taxed. Figuring out which percentage has already been taxed, and which percentage is taxable, can be a headache.
In the case of annuities, there's another complication: High fees built into many (but not all) tax-deferred annuities further weaken the case for buying them.

The critics point out that with lower capital gains taxes, it can actually cost you money to be in one of these accounts. That's because if you invest within an IRA or an annuity in the kind of investment that results in a capital gain, such as a growth stock, you can convert the tax on that gain from a (to-be-reduced) capital gains tax into a presumably higher income tax. But are they right?

Sometimes yes and sometimes no, and it depends in large part on your own tax circumstances and on your taste in investments. But one thing is certain: Tax-deferred compounding remains a very powerful tool that's hard to beat.

T. Rowe Price economist Joseph Healy recently compared the after-tax cash flow that you could get from a non-deductible IRA (an after-tax IRA in which income accumulated on a tax-deferred basis) to the income available from a taxable account. His conclusions?

A married couple who socked away the maximum $4,000 a year in an after-tax IRA for 20 years would have $369,296 upon retirement. If they saved the same amount in a regular investment account, they'd only have $238,151. If they then took 25 years to pull money out of that account, paying income tax on the buildup in the IRA as they withdrew the money, they'd have a 20-year stream of money equalling $607,066. Pulling money out of the smaller account would yield only $414,448, says Healy.

That's significant. But what if congressional Republicans have their way and cap capital gains at 20 percent instead of the current 28 percent rate? It would change Healy's results substantially only if your post-retirement tax rate were significantly above 20 percent, and most retirees find their average tax rates below that level. If you expect a low to moderate tax rate in retirement, you still can do well to defer taxes as long as possible.
If you're well off, expect to accumulate more than you can spend in your lifetime and have concerns about a higher post-retirement tax rate, the answers are not so simple.

First of all, your tax rate might be significantly higher than the capital gains rate. Experts at Ernst & Young have pointed out that if you buy individual growth stocks, you don't have to pay taxes on them until you sell them, so the net effect is like tax-deferred compounding.

Furthermore, individual shares of stock pass to heirs in an estate without being subject to capital gains taxes. If you buy a stock for $10, hold it for 20 years and sell it for $100, you'll pay a gains tax on that $90 profit. But if you bequeath that share to your heirs and die holding it, they get what's called a "step up in basis." The $100 is counted in the estate, and there's no tax on the gain. There's no federal tax at all unless the total estate exceeds the $600,000 estate-tax exemption.

If you really have a lot of money and worry about your heirs paying estate taxes and excess distribution taxes because there's too much money in your tax-deferred accounts, then stashing more in an IRA now is probably a bad decision.

If you're middling, have some money to invest in an IRA and some money to keep outside, consider Ernst & Young's advice: Keep growth stocks, low-turnover mutual funds and foreign stocks outside of the IRA. Use the IRA for high-dividend stocks, bonds, and actively traded mutual funds.
